title: The Agitation of the Soul and Demonic Strategy
english: a second shipwreck, harder than the first, will receive us, when the demon of vainglory blows against us. Wherefore our Lord in the Gospels, training the governing mind, says: ‘Take heed not to do your almsgiving before men to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward from your Father who is in the heavens.’ And again: ‘When you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, for they love to stand praying in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, so as to appear to men; truly I say to you, they have received their reward.’ And again he says: ‘When you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites; for they disfigure their faces so as to appear to men fasting; truly I say to you, they have received their reward.’

But here one must attend to the Physician of souls, how through almsgiving He heals thumos, through prayer He purifies the mind, and again through fasting He withers desire, from which the new man is composed, being renewed according to the image of Him who created him, in whom there is neither male nor female through holy dispassion, nor, through the one faith and love, Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, slave and free, but Christ is all things in all.

Chapter 4. One must inquire how the demons imprint and shape our ruling faculty in the phantasies during sleep; for such a thing seems to happen to the mind, whether seeing through eyes, or hearing through hearing, or again through some sense or other, or from the memory, which imprints the ruling faculty — not through the body, but moves those things which it received through the body. The demons, then, it seems to me, move the memory and imprint the ruling faculty; for the organ is held inactive by sleep. How, then, they again move the memory must be inquired — perhaps through the passions? And this is clear from the fact that the pure and dispassionate no longer suffer anything of the sort. There is also a certain simple movement produced by us or by holy powers, according to which we meet with saints in dreams and converse and feast together with them. Yet one must attend to this: that the images which the soul receives together with the body, these the memory moves without the body, and this is clear from the fact that often we suffer this even in dreams while the body is at rest.

For just as one may remember water both with thirst and without thirst, so one may remember gold both with greed and without greed, and likewise with other things. But for the mind to find differences between such and such phantasies is a mark of their evil craft.

And at the same time one must know this too: that the demons also use external things for their phantasies, as in the case of those sailing, with the sound of the waves. Our thumos, when moved contrary to nature, contributes greatly to the demons’ aim, and becomes most useful for all their scheming; hence none of them declines to trouble it by night and by day; but when they see it bound by gentleness, then they immediately release it under just pretexts, so that, having become sharper, it may serve their beastly thoughts; wherefore one must neither provoke it over just nor over unjust matters, nor give an evil sword to those who suggest them. Which I know many do often, and more than they should, being kindled by small pretexts.

Chapter 5. For over what, tell me, do you fall so quickly into battle, if you have despised foods and glory and money? And why do you feed the dog, you who profess to have nothing? But if it barks and attacks men, you are clearly shown to possess something within, and to wish to guard these things. But I am persuaded that such a one is far from pure prayer, knowing thumos to be the destroyer of such [prayer].

And besides these things I marvel, as though the saints were forgotten — David crying, ‘Cease from anger, and forsake thumos’ (Ps 37:8); the Preacher commanding, ‘Remove thumos from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh’ (Eccl 11:10); the Apostle commanding, ‘to lift up holy hands to the Lord in every place, without anger and doubting’ (1 Tim 2:8). And why do we not learn from the mystic and ancient custom of men, which drives the dogs out of the houses at the time of prayer, hinting at this: that thumos must not be present with those who pray? And again: ‘Their wine is the venom of dragons’ (Deut 32:33). The Nazirites abstained from wine.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction of thoughts
english: And one of the wise men from without declared gall and loin to be things not eaten by the gods — not knowing, I think, what he was saying; of which I myself consider the one a symbol of anger and the other of irrational desire.

But concerning the fact that one ought not be anxious about clothing or foods, I think it superfluous to write, since our Savior Himself forbade it in the Gospels: ‘For do not be anxious, He says, about your soul, what you will eat or what you will drink or what you will put on.’ For this is outright the mark of pagans and unbelievers, who reject the providence of the Master and deny the Creator; but such a thing is wholly foreign to Christians, who have once believed that even the two sparrows sold for a farthing are under the management of the holy angels. Yet this too is a habit of the demons: after the impure thoughts to cast in also those of anxiety, so that Jesus may withdraw, there being a crowd of notions in the place of the mind, and the word may become unfruitful, choked by the anxiety of thorns.

Chapter 6. Let us then, laying aside the thoughts from anxiety, cast our anxiety upon the Lord, being content with present things and using a poor life, and let us day by day strip off, along with our dress, the fathers of vainglory. But if anyone thinks it unseemly in poor dress, let him look at holy Paul in cold and nakedness, who awaited the crown of righteousness. But since the Apostle called this world a theater and a stadium, let us see whether it is possible, clothed in thoughts of anxiety, to run for the prize of the upward calling, or to wrestle against the principalities and powers and against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age; I do not know — being taught even by sensible experience. For that athlete will of course be hindered by his tunic and easily tripped, just as the mind is by the thoughts of anxiety — if he is a true [witness] who says that the mind clings to its own treasure: ‘For where your treasure is, He says, there will your heart be also.’

Chapter 7. Of the thoughts, some cut and some are cut; the evil cut the good, and the evil are in turn cut by the good. The Holy Spirit, then, attends to the thought first set forth, and judges or accepts us according to it. What I mean is this: I have a certain thought of hospitality, and I have it for the Lord’s sake; but when the tempter comes, it is cut — he suggests entertaining for the sake of glory.

Again: I have a thought of hospitality aimed at appearing to men; but this too, when a stronger thought comes, is cut through — [the thought] directing our virtue more toward the Lord and compelling us not to do these things for men. If, then, through our works we henceforth remain in the former [thoughts] while being tempted by the latter, we shall have the rewards of the former thoughts alone when they were set forth, because, being men and wrestling with demons, we cannot always keep the right thought incorrupt, nor again keep the evil thought untried, having acquired the seeds of virtues.

Yet if any of the cutting thoughts lingers, it settles in the region of the one being tempted, and henceforth the man, moved according to that thought, will act. We have learned with much observation that this is the difference between angelic thoughts, human ones, and those from demons: first, the angelic investigate the natures of things and trace out their spiritual logoi.

For example: for whose sake gold came to be, and why it is sandy, and how it is scattered somewhere below among the parts of the earth, and is found with much toil and labor; and how, once found, it is washed with water and handed to fire, and thus falls into the hands of craftsmen — those who make the lampstand of the tabernacle, and the censer, and the bowls and the cups, from which the Babylonian king no longer drinks now through the grace of our Savior — while Cleopas bears a heart burning from these mysteries.

But the demonic thought neither knows nor understands these things; it only suggests the acquisition of sensible gold, and foretells the luxury and glory to come from it; but the human thought seeks neither the acquisition nor investigates of what the gold is a symbol, but only brings into the mind the bare form of gold, separated from the passion of greed; but the…

title: The Combat with Demons and the Hatred of Evil
english: The same account will be given for the other things as well, by one who trains himself mystically against this evil one.

Chapter 8. There is a demon called the wanderer, who stands by the brothers especially toward dawn; he leads the recluse’s mind about from city to city and from house to house and from village to village — first, supposedly, making mere visits, meeting certain acquaintances and talking at length, corrupting his own state toward those he meets, and becoming distant, little by little taking forgetfulness of the knowledge of God and of virtue and of his calling. The recluse must, then, watch him: whence he begins and where he ends; for he does not work that long circuit idly or by chance, but wanting to corrupt the recluse’s state, he does these things so that the mind, inflamed by them and intoxicated by the many encounters, may straightway fall to the demon of fornication or of anger or of sadness, which most ruin the brightness of his state. But we, if we aim to know his craftiness clearly, must not speak to him hastily nor show that we know what is happening — how he works the encounters in the mind and in what way he drives the mind little by little toward death, since he will flee from us; for he does not consent to be seen doing these things; and henceforth we shall know nothing of what we were eager to learn. But let us allow him even one more day, or a second, to complete the drama, so that, having learned his awkwardness precisely, we may thereafter refute him with a word and put him to flight.

Chapter 9. But since it happens that in the time of temptation the mind, being clouded, does not see clearly what is happening, let this be done after the demon’s withdrawal: sitting by yourself, remember the things that happened to you — whence you began and where you went, and in what place you were seized by the spirit of fornication or of anger or of sadness, and how all that happened came to pass — and learn these things clearly, and hand them to your memory so that you may have wherewith to refute him as he approaches, and denounce the place hidden by him, and henceforth you will not follow him. But if you ever wish to provoke him even to madness, refute him as soon as he stands by, and reveal the first place into which he entered, and the second, and the third — for he rages greatly, not bearing the shame; and the proof that you spoke to him at the right moment will be that the thought has fled from you; for henceforth it is impossible for him to stand when clearly refuted.

When this demon of wandering is defeated, there succeeds a very heavy sleep, and numbness with much coldness of the eyelids, and endless yawns, and shoulders weighed down and growing numb — which the Holy Spirit will dissolve by intense prayer.

Chapter 10. Hatred against the demons contributes greatly to our salvation, and is fit for the working of virtue; but we cannot nourish this in ourselves as some good offspring, since the pleasure-loving spirits destroy it and call the soul back again to friendship and familiarity; but this friendship — or rather, this hard-to-heal gangrene — the Physician of souls heals by abandonment; for He allows us to suffer something fearful from them by night or by day, and again the soul runs back to its original hatred, taught to say to the Lord, according to David: ‘I have hated them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me’ (Ps 139:22). For he hates the enemies with perfect hatred who sins neither in deed nor in thought; which is the proof of the first and greatest dispassion.

Chapter 11. But concerning the demon who makes the soul insensible, what need is there to speak? For I fear even to write about him — how the soul is displaced from its own state; for at the time of his visitation it strips off the fear of God and reverence, and reckons sin not to be sin, and does not consider lawlessness to be lawlessness, and remembers punishment and eternal judgment as a bare word, and truly mocks at the fire-bearing earthquake, and supposedly confesses God but does not know what He commanded; you beat upon the breast while it moves toward sin, and it does not feel.
